question: In 1974 the American economist Anne Krueger published a famous paper that gave the world the phrase 'rent-seeking' -- when people spend real effort chasing government-granted privileges (like a license or a monopoly) instead of producing goods. She used one country as her main example. Its heavy use of import licenses in the 1960s and 1970s meant businesses spent enormous time hiring lobbyists and cultivating officials just to get a permit. Which country did Krueger study?
context: India in the 1960s-70s used import licenses to allocate scarce foreign exchange. Firms lobbied intensively for licenses (which conveyed enormous scarcity rent). Krueger's paper also included Turkish data. Source: aeaweb.org (Krueger 1974).

question: In 1980 Basic Books published a book by Thomas Sowell. It took the central argument from Hayek's 1945 essay -- that useful knowledge is spread across many heads and cannot be centralized -- and expanded it with real-world examples for regular readers. Hayek himself endorsed the book. What was Sowell's title?
context: Sowell's Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books, 1980) is explicitly built on Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.' Hayek endorsed it as expanding admirably on his original concepts. The book won the 1980 Law and Economics Center Prize. The three distractors are all real later Sowell books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_and_Decisions.

question: Back in 2013, a small group of Bitcoin developers wrote down the standard rulebook for turning a wallet's secret number into a friendly list of English words. Anyone who follows the rule can read anyone else's backup -- that is why it works across every brand. The rule became one of the numbered Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs), the technical documents that shape the network. Which numbered proposal is the seed-phrase rule?
context: BIP-39 (Marek Palatinus, Pavol Rusnak, Aaron Voisine, Sean Bowe; 2013) defines the mnemonic backup. BIP-32 defines hierarchical deterministic key trees; BIP-141 added SegWit in 2015; BIP-9 concerned soft-fork version signalling. Source: https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki.

question: In 1946 an American businessman named Leonard Read grew worried that most Americans no longer understood how free markets create wealth. He started the first big American organization set up to teach free-market economics to teachers, students, and businessmen. What was the group called?
context: FEE, founded 1946, preceded the Reason Foundation (1968), the Cato Institute (1977), and the Mises Institute (1982). Source: grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_for_Economic_Education.

question: By 1934 Vienna was no longer safe for the Jewish Austrian-school economist Ludwig von Mises -- the Nazi movement was rising next door in Germany, and Austria itself would be annexed four years later. Mises accepted a teaching post at a graduate institute in a French-speaking Swiss city, where he would spend the rest of the decade before fleeing again to America. In which Swiss city did Mises land?
context: The Institut universitaire de hautes etudes internationales (IUHEI) in Geneva was one of the few European institutions still hiring Vienna-Jewish scholars in the mid-1930s. Zurich, Bern, and Basel all had universities but not the IUHEI. Mises left Geneva in 1940 when the fall of France made continental Europe untenable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises.

question: In 1998 the American computer scientist Nick Szabo shared an essay on a cypherpunk mailing list. He described a way to make rare digital tokens by solving hard math puzzles. The tokens would be scarce like real gold pulled from the earth, but they would live only in software. What did Szabo call his invention?
context: Szabo drafted bit gold in 1998; a blog post appeared in 2005. b-money is Wei Dai's separate 1998 proposal; Hashcash is Adam Back's 1997 anti-spam PoW; DigiCash is David Chaum's 1989 company. Source: https://unenumerated.blogspot.com/2005/12/bit-gold.html.

question: In 1979 President Jimmy Carter appointed Paul Volcker to chair the Federal Reserve with orders to break the double-digit inflation choking the US economy. Volcker's plan was harsh: choke off money growth by driving interest rates as high as it took. The federal funds rate — the Fed's key overnight lending rate — spiked sharply, peaking in June and July of 1981. What was the peak rate?
context: The federal funds rate peaked at about 20.06% in July 1981, per FRED data. It was the highest US policy rate of the postwar era. Source: Grokipedia 'Federal funds rate' (2026-09-05).

question: The American economist Thomas Sowell boiled James Buchanan's whole public-choice point down to a two-word question a critic should always ask. Whenever someone says 'the market has failed here, so government must step in,' Sowell says the honest listener should always ask this. What are Sowell's two words?
context: Sowell's 'compared to what?' recurs across Knowledge and Decisions (1980), The Vision of the Anointed (1995), and other books. It is his shorthand for the Buchanan comparative move. Source: Sowell, Knowledge and Decisions (Basic Books 1980).

question: In the early 1870s three economists working in three different countries — Carl Menger in Austria, William Stanley Jevons in England, and Leon Walras in France — each stumbled onto the same big idea on their own, without knowing about each other. Value, they said, comes not from the total stock of a thing but from the extra use of just the very next unit. Historians of economics now give this joint discovery one name. What is this cluster of near-simultaneous breakthroughs called?
context: William Stanley Jevons in England and Leon Walras in Switzerland reached the marginal-utility insight independently of Menger and of each other; none of the three knew the others were working on it. It stands with Darwin-Wallace natural selection (1858) and Leibniz-Newton calculus as one of history's clearest cases of parallel scientific invention. The Methodenstreit was Menger's LATER 1883 methodological quarrel with Schmoller; the Keynesian Revolution was 1936; the Neoclassical Synthesis was Samuelson's 1940s-50s fusion. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalism; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principles_of_Economics_(Menger_book).

question: In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a fake petition addressed to the French Chamber of Deputies, mocking protectionist industries that begged the government to block foreign competition. In his satirical petition, the fake petitioners begged the government to shut out one utterly 'unfair rival' -- the Sun itself, whose free light was ruining their sales. Which trade did the pretend petitioners claim to be from?
context: Full title: 'Petition of the Manufacturers of Candles, Waxlights, Lamps, Candlesticks, Street Lamps, Snuffers, Extinguishers, and the Producers of Oil, Tallow, Rosin, Alcohol, and, generally, of Everything Connected with Lighting.' Bastiat published it under his own name, not anonymously. Source: mises.org/library/candlemakers-petition.

question: The Austrian School's most famous German term -- Grenznutzen, 'edge-usefulness' -- appears nowhere in Menger's 1871 Principles. It was coined thirteen years later, in an 1884 book by one of Menger's two great pupils. When the term was translated back into English, it became the phrase every economics textbook now teaches. Who coined Grenznutzen?
context: Wieser (1851-1926) coined Grenznutzen in his 1884 Uber den Ursprung und die Hauptgesetze des wirtschaftlichen Werthes to name a concept his teacher had already articulated in prose. English 'marginal utility' is a direct back-translation of Wieser's coinage. Boehm-Bawerk, Menger's other great pupil, developed capital and interest theory; Menger wrote before the term existed; Walras wrote in French. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Friedrich_von_Wieser.

question: Imagine you have five dollars in your pocket and you walk up to a snack shop. You can spend it on a comic book OR on an ice cream cone -- the shop will not sell you both for that price. If you buy the comic, the ice cream you gave up is called the ___ of your choice. Economists have a special name for what you sacrificed.
context: Wieser held the Vienna chair from 1903 to 1922. He also served as Austro-Hungarian Minister of Commerce in 1917-1918. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_von_Wieser.
